answers.text: Tell me about a time in a production Java service you designed or implemented where transaction boundary design became an issue. Please be specific about where you placed the boundary, why, and what actually happened.
answers.answer: On our tax-assessment service, I ran into a boundary problem processing refund calculations. Originally the whole assessment -- validate the return, compute the refund, write the refund record, and call our internal audit-flagging service -- ran in one @Transactional method. During the March filing surge, when we process about 40,000 returns a day instead of the usual 5,000, transactions blocked on the same taxpayer_accounts row for up to 600ms whenever the audit-flagging call was slow. I moved the audit call outside the transaction: the assessment and refund write commit together, since those two must be atomic, and I write a queued 'needs audit check' row in the same transaction instead of calling out synchronously. Assessment latency at p99 dropped from about 1.4 seconds to 220ms during peak. The failure I hit afterward: the audit queue itself backed up 3,000 rows deep during one surge because I hadn't sized its consumer for peak volume, so I added a second consumer instance.
answers.says: Names a concrete transaction-boundary problem in a production Java service they were responsible for (e.g., lock contention on a long transaction, an external API call left inside a transaction, inconsistency from an isolation level), describes where they moved the boundary and the grounds for that decision (measurements, a real incident, data-consistency requirements), and covers the outcome or the fix for a failure, with numbers and time frames. Beyond just ‘we did it as a team,’ their own judgment and hands-on work are clear, and they can explain a design failure in their own words.

answers.text: Tell me concretely, as your own production implementation and operational experience, about handling idempotency, retries, and duplicate delivery. Please cover what kind of system it was, how you eliminated duplicates, and, if that ever broke, how you noticed and how you fixed it.
answers.answer: On TaxCore, every refund disbursement carries an idempotency key made from the taxpayer's filing ID plus the tax year, enforced with a unique constraint in a disbursements table, so a retried disbursement request after a timeout returns the existing record instead of issuing a second payment. This broke about three years ago: our payment processor's callback endpoint started timing out under load during a surge, and our retry logic resent 85 disbursement requests over about five hours with a bug that generated a new filing-ID-plus-year key each time, due to a data-type mismatch in how the tax year was formatted between two of our internal services. I found it during our weekly reconciliation, which showed 85 taxpayers with two disbursement records instead of one, totaling about $142,000 in duplicate payments. I corrected each with a reversing entry, not a deletion, and fixed the formatting mismatch so key generation was consistent across both services.
answers.says: Names the concrete mechanism they implemented and operated (idempotency-key design, store choice, duplicate-delivery detection, reconciliation mechanism), why they chose that design, and the process of noticing and recovering when an incident or duplication actually occurred, with numbers (scale, count, time taken) and time frames. If it was an experience of resolving a consistency mismatch, they can also describe the root-cause triage and the grounds for correcting it with a new journal entry or record rather than an overwrite.

answers.text: Tell me about your experience and thinking on migrating from Java to Rust. If you have production Rust experience, tell me its scope; if not, tell me how you think you could realistically learn the differences from Java — ownership, lifetimes, async runtimes. Also tell me your thinking on how to decide a service boundary.
answers.answer: I haven't written Rust, in production or otherwise, so I want to be upfront about that rather than talk around it. If I were building a realistic plan, I'd start with the official book and Rustlings over the first month, alongside rewriting something small I already understand well -- probably our refund-calculation logic, since I know its edge cases from having built it in Java -- to force myself to hit ownership and borrowing for real. I'd expect the first two months to be mostly fighting the compiler on things that are simple in Java, and I wouldn't feel ready to own a production boundary until I'd built at least one real async service end to end, maybe four to six months in. On migration generally, I'd want to move a small, stateless, well-tested piece first and run it alongside the Java version rather than trust a rewrite immediately, which is closer to how I approach any risky change, language aside.
answers.says: If they have production Rust experience, they describe which part of production it was (e.g., why latency became an issue, how they cut the boundary with Java, the measurement results), with numbers and time frames, and can describe failures too. If they lack production experience, they explain the concrete differences from Java in ownership, lifetimes, and async runtimes in their own words, and describe a realistic learning plan (what they have already written, read, or been studying). In addition, they state a view that fits our approach — deciding a boundary and migrating while measuring, rather than a full rewrite — together with their own grounds for it.

answers.text: If you were to move part of the ledger write path to Rust, where would you start, where would you place the boundary with Java, and what would you measure before and after the migration to make that call? If you've cut out a language or service boundary before, please answer in light of that experience.
answers.answer: Without Rust experience myself, I'd still apply the same approach I used moving the audit-flagging call out of our transaction: find the least stateful, most isolated piece of the write path first, something like fee or interest calculation that takes inputs and returns a number without needing to touch the database directly, and put that behind an interface the Java side calls. I'd run it in parallel with the existing Java calculation for some weeks, logging both results, and only cut over once outputs matched consistently. What I'd watch: latency of the new call, error rate, and a count of any mismatches against the Java result. I don't have my own experience carving this particular kind of boundary in Rust, so I'd want a more experienced Rust engineer to sanity-check the interface design before I trusted my own judgment on it fully.
answers.says: Concretely describes how to choose a migration target (measuring hot paths, starting with lower-risk parts), how to place the boundary (the shape of the interface, how to keep data consistent, coexisting with Java), and what metrics to watch before and after migration (latency, memory, correctness reconciliation), together with their own grounds for those decisions. If they've carved out a boundary before, they include the numbers, failures, and how they built agreement with the team. Fits our ‘decide the boundary before you rewrite’ approach, and can also describe how they resisted the temptation to do a full rewrite.

answers.text: Have you ever, while responding to an urgent incident, felt tempted to skip review or the normal deployment procedure? Tell me what you actually did, and what you think would need to be in place to justify a decision to skip a step.
answers.answer: During the interest-double-application incident, I was tempted to skip the normal review step and push the scheduler fix immediately once I found it, since statements were going out that evening. I didn't skip it: I posted in our team channel, got a colleague to review the one-line scheduler config change over a ten-minute call instead of our usual next-day review cycle, and got it merged and deployed within that window. I think the key thing that made review possible even under time pressure was that the fix itself was small and easy to reason about quickly, which isn't always true. I'd only consider actually skipping review if getting even a fast second opinion were genuinely impossible and real harm were actively accumulating, and I'd want to announce that decision and log it clearly rather than quietly doing it and explaining later, which I haven't personally had to do.
answers.says: Names a concrete experience of being forced to choose between the procedure and an emergency, and describes what they actually did. If they skipped it, they describe the steps — announcing it beforehand, recording it afterward, and following up with the normal procedure once recovered — together with the criteria for that skip decision. If they didn't skip it, they describe why (not shipping a change they can't verify, money is not a test environment) and an alternative way to move quickly and safely without cutting the procedure. Either way, their own judgment and its outcome come through as a concrete example.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you shared a mistake or a delay early, and about your experience with on-call, handling inquiries, or mentoring juniors. For both, please be concrete about what you yourself did.
answers.answer: I once shipped a rounding change to how we calculate late-payment penalties that was technically correct but changed the result for about 200 existing draft assessments in a way I hadn't checked before deploying. I found the discrepancy myself the next day while spot-checking an unrelated ticket, and reported it to my lead that same afternoon along with the affected count, rather than waiting to see if anyone else noticed first. On on-call: I've been on our rotation for about five years, one week in six, and I handle taxpayer-facing incident escalations directly rather than just paging someone else. I also mentor one junior engineer currently, mostly through code review and walking through incidents like the scheduler one together after the fact, and I've never seen on-call or that kind of mentoring time as separate from the actual engineering work.
answers.says: Can describe a concrete example of sharing their own mistake or delay before it got worse — what, when, to whom, how it was communicated, and what happened as a result. Also names a real example of taking on on-call rotation, inquiry handling, or mentoring juniors as their own job (duration, frequency, approach), and can describe never having thought of it as ‘not my real job.’ Both are told as their own actions, including experience of sharing within a blameless culture.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a team's technical decision. How did you voice the disagreement, how was it decided, and what did you do after the decision was made?
answers.answer: About two years ago, a colleague proposed rewriting our refund-calculation module from scratch, arguing the existing code was too hard to follow. I disagreed with a full rewrite and instead pulled our incident history, showing we'd had exactly one bug in that module in three years, plus an estimate of the two to three months a rewrite would take against other backlog work. The team discussed it and decided against the full rewrite, opting instead for me to refactor the module's worst-documented section incrementally over a few weeks while leaving the rest alone. I did that refactor as agreed and didn't go back and quietly rewrite the rest of it afterward, even though I still think parts of it could be cleaner, because the team's call was that the risk of a rewrite wasn't worth it for code that wasn't actually causing problems.
answers.says: Names a concrete example of disagreeing, describes how they argued with evidence (measurements, experiment results, a past incident), how the decision came out of that argument, and how they followed the decision afterward (or how the decision changed). Can also describe not overturning it alone after the fact, or, if they nearly did, how they stopped themselves. If they've ever argued for a full rewrite out of technical preference, they can describe how they held that impulse in check.

answers.text: Have you ever felt tempted to use production data or balances to check that something worked? What did you actually do in that situation? When something can't be reproduced in a test environment, how do you go about verifying it?
answers.answer: I've wanted to check something against real production balances more than once, most clearly during the disbursement duplicate-payment issue, and what I did was take that week's disbursements and filing records, strip taxpayer names and account numbers, and run my grouping query against that masked copy in a separate database rather than live. For the scheduler-duplication incident, where I needed to confirm the startup check actually prevented a second run under real conditions, I tested that in staging by deliberately triggering a duplicate scheduler trigger there, rather than trying to reproduce it in production at all. The one time I checked a live number directly was confirming the $3.20-per-account average from the interest incident, which I did with a read-only query and mentioned in our incident channel before running it, since I wanted the number for the postmortem rather than to change anything.
answers.says: Names a concrete situation where they were tempted to check something in production, and describes the method they actually used (reproducing it on a masked copy, comparing via shadow execution, a read-only reconciliation, a canary), the grounds for that decision, and the cost it took. If they had no choice but to check in production, they can also describe how they announced it, recorded it, and limited the impact.

answers.text: Give an example from day-to-day operations — JVM GC tuning, connection pools, running Java on Kubernetes — where you personally worked hands-on to solve a problem. Tell me what you measured, what you changed, and what changed as a result.
answers.answer: We had connection pool exhaustion on the same service during that same March surge, before I made the transaction fix. HikariCP wait times hit 900ms at p95, and I pulled pool metrics from Grafana showing all 25 connections were in use for stretches of 2-3 seconds at a time, correlated with the slow audit calls I mentioned. Before I understood the root cause, my first move was just raising pool size from 25 to 50, which briefly helped the wait metric but pushed our database's own connection limit close to its ceiling of 200 total across all services, so I reverted that within a day. The actual fix was the transaction-boundary change, which reduced how long connections were held per request; after that, pool wait dropped to under 30ms at p95 even at the same peak volume, without needing more connections at all.
answers.says: Names a concrete operational problem in a Java service they operated (e.g., latency degradation from GC pauses, connection pool exhaustion, an OOM on Kubernetes), and describes the measurement tools used, the numbers obtained, the changes tried, the results (with figures), and, if the first fix missed, the failure and the retry. Can explain the triage process in their own words, with grounds for the decisions rather than a list of tool names.

fit.says: Considering what it would be like for this person to work here, they can be judged as someone who would act in line with all of our working principles (argue with evidence, then follow the decision; do not hide; money is not a test environment; operations and support are equal work; decide the boundary before you rewrite). Throughout the candidate's account of their experience, they consistently show a stance of sharing incidents and mistakes without hiding them, treating on-call, support, and mentoring juniors as their own job, never skipping review and deployment procedures even in an emergency, and carrying out migrations based on measurement and agreement while respecting the team's decisions.
